Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: A junctional rhythm due to sick sinus syndrome or high-grade atrioventricular block is treated with what?
opts: Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. A junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome is already slow, so slowing it further is the opposite of the goal. Tell: block or sinus node failure behind a junctional rhythm calls for a permanent pacemaker.

Catheter ablation is used for tachycardias, such as focal atrial tachycardia, nodal reentry or an accessory pathway. A slow junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: ablation removes fast circuits; pacemakers support slow rhythms.

Correct. Management of junctional rhythm depends on the cause, and when it is due to complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or sick sinus syndrome, a permanent pacemaker is placed. Digoxin toxicity is instead treated with atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab (fragment antigen-binding), and asymptomatic healthy people need no treatment.

No treatment suits a junctional rhythm in an asymptomatic, otherwise healthy person, such as an athlete with high vagal tone. When the cause is high-grade atrioventricular block or sick sinus syndrome, a permanent pacemaker is needed. Tell: the cause decides, and block or sinus node disease means a pacemaker.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Why is adenosine useful when focal atrial tachycardia is suspected?
opts: Adenosine is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than nodal or accessory pathway reentry. That relative failure, not reliable termination, is what makes it diagnostic. Tell: if adenosine reliably stops the rhythm, think node-dependent reentry instead.

The usual cure for focal atrial tachycardia is catheter ablation, curative in about 90 percent; chronic management otherwise starts with an oral beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Adenosine is a diagnostic tool, not a cure. Tell: ablation cures the focus; adenosine helps identify it.

Adenosine is used acutely, not to prevent recurrences. Chronic focal atrial tachycardia is managed with an oral beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker as initial therapy, or with catheter ablation. Tell: prevention means oral drugs or ablation; adenosine is diagnostic.

Correct. Adenosine is an important diagnostic tool when focal atrial tachycardia is suspected because it is usually less effective at terminating it than the reentry tachycardias that depend on the atrioventricular node. A tachycardia that persists despite adenosine therefore points toward an atrial focus.

set1.q: Which is a listed risk factor for atrial fibrillation?
opts: Correct. Sleep apnea is a listed risk; atrial fibrillation is commonly seen in patients with hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, a family history of atrial fibrillation, obesity, sleep apnea, excessive alcohol and older age.

Hypothyroidism is listed as a cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, not among the atrial fibrillation risks. Tell: the atrial fibrillation list includes sleep apnea and obesity alongside hypertension and diabetes; thyroid underactivity sits on the slow-rhythm list.

Obesity, not low body weight, is the listed weight-related risk for atrial fibrillation. The others are hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, family history, sleep apnea, excessive alcohol and older age. Tell: excess weight, not low weight, raises the risk.

Atrial fibrillation is commonly seen in the elderly, so older age, not youth, is the listed age-related risk. Sleep apnea, obesity, hypertension and diabetes are on the list too. Tell: think of older patients with metabolic and sleep problems.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What is the first-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Adenosine is the second step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, used if a vagal maneuver fails, and it may be repeated once. It may convert the rhythm to normal sinus rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Tell: first line means before any drug, which is the vagal maneuver.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, the less common presentation. A stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver. Tell: the word stable points to the vagal maneuver; unstable points to the shock.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the setting in which adenosine must never be used. Ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver. Tell: procainamide answers pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not routine supraventricular tachycardia.

Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver. Adenosine follows, and may be repeated once, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to see P waves; a hemodynamically unstable patient instead gets immediate synchronized cardioversion.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, so giving one would slow this patient further. Beta blockers belong in fast rhythms, such as rate control for stable atrial flutter. Tell: a hypotensive, confused patient with a slow sinus rhythm needs atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker.

Digoxin is listed with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia, so it would worsen this rhythm. Look for it as the culprit in a slow patient, not the rescue. Tell: drugs that cause bradycardia never treat it; atropine does.

Correct. A slow sinus rhythm causing hypotension and confusion is acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, and atropine is first line. If it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows; chronic symptomatic bradycardia is treated with a permanent pacemaker instead.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia, after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing is the opposite of what an unstable bradycardia needs. Tell: adenosine is for a fast narrow rhythm; atropine is for a slow, unstable one.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, but it is not the named most-common tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: the fast phase is classically irregularly irregular without P waves, which is fibrillation, not a regular sawtooth.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the tachyarrhythmia in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, who then need a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. It is not the most common one; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most-common answer.

Sinus tachycardia is a regular rhythm at over 100 to 160 with a P wave before every QRS, usually driven by a physiologic or pathologic process. The fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome is most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus rhythm. Tell: the named most-common tachyarrhythmia is irregularly irregular without P waves.

Correct. Tachy-brady syndrome is the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses. The most common cause of the fast phase is atrial fibrillation, which appears as an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What is the usual rate of atrial fibrillation?
opts: A rate of 40 to 60 is the usual rate of a junctional rhythm, a regular rhythm with inverted or hidden P waves. Atrial fibrillation usually runs faster, at 110 to 160, and is irregularly irregular. Tell: 40 to 60 is junctional; 110 to 160 is the usual atrial fibrillation range.

A rate of 60 to 100 is the normal sinus range, also seen in sinus arrhythmia. Atrial fibrillation usually runs faster, at 110 to 160, though it can be slower. Tell: 60 to 100 is a sinus number; the usual atrial fibrillation rate starts at 110.

Correct. Atrial fibrillation usually runs at 110 to 160, though not always: the rate can fall below 80 or rise above 200. The rhythm is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, no PR interval and a narrow QRS.

An atrial rate of 250 or more, approaching 300, describes the sawtooth waves of atrial flutter. The usual ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation is 110 to 160. Tell: 250 to 300 is a flutter atrial rate; 110 to 160 is the atrial fibrillation rate.

set1.q: In whom are the symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia more pronounced?
opts: Correct. Symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia, such as palpitations, lightheadedness, dyspnea and chest discomfort, may be more pronounced in the elderly and in those with underlying structural heart disease. Many patients are otherwise asymptomatic or have only transient symptoms.

Young, healthy people are not the group named for more pronounced symptoms; the elderly and those with underlying structural heart disease are. Patients may otherwise be asymptomatic or have only transient symptoms. Tell: age and heart disease amplify the symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia may cause only transient symptoms, so the paroxysmal pattern is not what makes symptoms worse. Older age and underlying structural heart disease do. Tell: paroxysmal means episodes come and go; pronounced symptoms track age and heart disease.

Women are affected far more than men by atrioventricular nodal reentry, but that describes who gets one subtype, not whose symptoms are more pronounced. Symptoms are worse in the elderly and in those with structural heart disease. Tell: sex predicts nodal reentry; age and heart disease predict symptom severity.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which physical finding fits atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia?
opts: Absent leg pulses are not a feature of nodal reentry. The examination clue listed for atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is visible neck pulsations, the frog sign, along with sudden-onset palpitations. Tell: in nodal reentry, look at the neck, not the legs.

Correct. Patients with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia typically complain of sudden-onset palpitations and neck pulsations, seen on examination as the frog sign. The rhythm is a regular, narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves from a reentry circuit within the node.

Kussmaul sign is not the examination finding listed for nodal reentry. That finding is visible neck pulsations, the frog sign, with sudden-onset palpitations, in a regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves. Tell: in nodal reentry the neck visibly pulsates during the tachycardia.

Pulsus paradoxus is not the examination finding listed for nodal reentry. Patients with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia typically show visible neck pulsations, the frog sign, along with sudden palpitations. Tell: the frog sign is the named bedside clue to nodal reentry.

set1.q: What defines long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation?
opts: Continuous for 7 days to a year

Continuous atrial fibrillation for more than 7 days but less than one year is persistent atrial fibrillation, which needs treatment. It becomes long-standing persistent only after more than a year. Tell: the one-year mark separates persistent from long-standing persistent.

Episodes lasting under a week that usually end without treatment are paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation is continuous for over a year. Tell: under a week and self-ending is paroxysmal.

A joint decision by patient and clinician to stop trying to restore or maintain sinus rhythm defines permanent atrial fibrillation. Long-standing persistent is defined by duration, continuous for more than a year. Tell: permanent is a decision; long-standing persistent is a duration.

Correct. Long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation is continuous for more than one year. Paroxysmal lasts under a week and usually ends without treatment, persistent is continuous for over 7 days but under a year and needs treatment, and permanent is defined by a joint decision rather than by duration.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is more common in whom?
opts: Men are the less affected group; atrioventricular nodal reentry is far more common in women than in men. Tell: picture the typical patient as a woman without heart disease who has sudden palpitations and neck pulsations.

Severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, especially when acutely ill, is the setting of multifocal atrial tachycardia. Nodal reentry is far more common in women and is commonly seen without heart disease. Tell: lung disease points to multifocal atrial tachycardia; a woman with a normal heart points to nodal reentry.

Prior heart surgery causes atrial scarring that sets up atrial flutter, and injury to the sinus node that causes sick sinus syndrome. Nodal reentry is commonly seen without heart disease and far more often in women. Tell: surgery points to flutter or sick sinus syndrome; a normal heart in a woman points to nodal reentry.

Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia affects women far more than men and is commonly seen without heart disease. It may occur spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: How is a junctional rhythm generally tolerated?
opts: Correct. A junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated. Management depends on the cause: no treatment for an asymptomatic, otherwise healthy person, a permanent pacemaker for complete or high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome, and atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab (fragment antigen-binding) for digitalis toxicity.

Syncope is not the usual course; a junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated and can even be seen in healthy athletes with increased vagal tone. Tell: generally well tolerated is the stated rule, and treatment is driven by the cause, not by the rhythm itself.

A junctional rhythm is not described as progressing to ventricular fibrillation; it is generally well tolerated, and a healthy person needs no treatment. Progression to ventricular fibrillation is the named risk of 1:1 atrial flutter. Tell: the rhythm with a big risk of ventricular fibrillation is 1:1 flutter, not a junctional rhythm.

Only a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or sick sinus syndrome needs a permanent pacemaker. Most junctional rhythms are generally well tolerated, and an asymptomatic, otherwise healthy person needs no treatment. Tell: the cause, not the rhythm itself, decides on a pacemaker.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: Which is a listed cause of junctional rhythm?
opts: Anemia is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, a compensatory fast sinus rhythm. Junctional rhythm follows sinus node failure, inferior infarction, cardiac surgery or digoxin toxicity. Tell: anemia speeds the sinus node rather than letting the junction take over.

Correct. Digoxin toxicity is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, along with sinus node dysfunction such as sick sinus syndrome or significant bradycardia, inferior myocardial infarction and the acute period after cardiac surgery. Junctional rhythm from digitalis toxicity is treated with atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab (fragment antigen-binding).

Hyperthyroidism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, speeding the sinus node. A junctional rhythm appears when the sinus node fails or with digoxin toxicity. Tell: thyroid excess belongs on the sinus tachycardia list, not the junctional one.

Caffeine is a listed trigger of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and of premature atrial contractions, both fast or early-beat problems. It is not among the causes of a slow junctional rhythm. Tell: caffeine provokes fast rhythms; digoxin toxicity produces a slow junctional one.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: For stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia, which acute drugs are used?
opts: Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. Focal atrial tachycardia is fast, so raising the rate is the opposite of the goal. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable rhythms; stable focal atrial tachycardia gets an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

Intravenous magnesium is not among the listed acute treatments for focal atrial tachycardia. A stable, symptomatic patient gets an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, and amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion. Tell: stable focal atrial tachycardia is rate controlled intravenously.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia gets an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: procainamide belongs to pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not to a single atrial focus.

Correct. Hemodynamically stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia is treated acutely with an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, while the underlying cause or precipitating factors are found and treated. Synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability, and amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Besides drugs and thyroid disease, which condition is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Pain and anxiety are listed physiologic causes of sinus tachycardia, raising the sinus rate rather than slowing it. Tell: stress responses speed the heart, while raised intracranial pressure slows it.

Hypoxia is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, not bradycardia. The non-drug, non-thyroid causes of sinus bradycardia include increased intracranial pressure, sinus node ischemia and late-stage infection. Tell: hypoxia speeds the sinus rate.

Correct. Increased intracranial pressure is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, together with sinus node ischemia, late-stage infection, hypothyroidism and the drugs beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. Sinus bradycardia can also be a normal variant in athletes, during sleep and in adults over 65.

Pulmonary embolism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, along with hypoxia, shock and myocardial infarction. It does not appear among the causes of sinus bradycardia. Tell: pulmonary embolism goes with a fast sinus rate; raised intracranial pressure with a slow one.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which P wave finding fits atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia?
opts: Correct. In atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia the P waves are hidden or retrograde and the PR interval is hidden or short, in a regular rhythm above 100 and usually 200 to 300. In the orthodromic form the retrograde P wave falls after a normal-width QRS.

Sawtooth flutter waves belong to atrial flutter, at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. In atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia the P waves are hidden or retrograde. Tell: sawtooth means flutter; retrograde or hidden P waves mean reentry.

Three or more P-wave shapes in one lead mark multifocal atrial tachycardia, an irregular rhythm from multiple foci. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is regular with hidden or retrograde P waves. Tell: changing P shapes mean multiple foci; hidden or retrograde P waves mean a reentry loop.
One upright P before each QRS

One uniform P wave before every QRS describes a sinus rhythm, such as sinus tachycardia. In atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia the P waves are hidden or retrograde. Tell: an upright P wave in front is sinus; a P wave after the QRS or none at all suggests reentry.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which condition is a pathologic cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Hypovolemia is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, along with hypotension, anemia and hypoxia. It speeds the sinus rate rather than slowing it. Tell: volume loss makes the heart race; an underactive thyroid slows it.

Correct. Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, with sinus node ischemia, increased intracranial pressure, late-stage infection and drugs such as beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. Sinus bradycardia can be either pathological or a normal variant.

Hyperthyroidism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia. It is the underactive thyroid, hypothyroidism, that is listed among the causes of sinus bradycardia. Tell: hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus node; hypothyroidism slows it.

Anemia is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, like hypovolemia and hypoxia. It does not slow the sinus rate. Tell: anemia belongs on the fast list; hypothyroidism belongs on the slow list.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated first with which?
opts: Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, a sustained rhythm. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol. Tell: amiodarone converts a tachycardia; a beta blocker settles symptomatic early beats.

Correct. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated. Catheter ablation is reserved for frequent beats or beats triggering atrial fibrillation, and asymptomatic ones need no treatment.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. It is not used to suppress premature atrial contractions. Tell: symptomatic premature atrial beats get a beta blocker.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions get a beta blocker. Tell: procainamide belongs to pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not to early atrial beats.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: In sinus arrhythmia, how does the heart rate change with breathing?
opts: A P-wave shape that varies in an irregular rhythm suggests multiple atrial foci, as in multifocal atrial tachycardia, which needs at least three shapes. Sinus arrhythmia keeps uniform P waves, and its rate does change, rising with inspiration and falling with expiration. Tell: in sinus arrhythmia the rate moves and the P wave stays the same.
Faster on inspiration, slower on expiration

Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern: the rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration. Every beat keeps a uniform P wave and a narrow QRS, and the rate stays within 60 to 100.
Slower on inspiration, faster on expiration

This reverses the pattern. In sinus arrhythmia the sinus rate rises during inspiration and falls during expiration, with uniform P waves throughout. Tell: inspiration speeds and expiration slows, so the beats crowd together as the breath comes in and spread apart as it goes out.
Faster in both phases of the breath

The rate does not rise throughout the breath; it rises with inspiration and falls with expiration, which is what makes sinus arrhythmia irregular with a pattern. A rate that stayed fast in both phases would simply be a faster sinus rhythm. Tell: the pattern has two directions, up on the way in and down on the way out.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: How is hemodynamically stable atrial flutter treated first?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter, and an elective outpatient cardioversion comes only after 21 days of anticoagulation. The question specifies a stable patient, who starts with rate control. Tell: stable flutter gets a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker first; unstable flutter gets the shock.

Catheter ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate, but it is not the first step for a stable patient. Stable flutter starts with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: the first step is rate control; ablation is the definitive end point.

Repeated adenosine belongs to the sequence for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, not to the listed treatment of atrial flutter. Stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. Tell: flutter has its own sequence, rate control if stable and synchronized cardioversion if unstable.

Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is treated first with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker, while an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion. Rate control is harder to achieve in flutter than in atrial fibrillation, and anticoagulation is part of management.

set1.q: Which drug is a direct oral anticoagulant preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation?
opts: Procainamide is an intravenous drug used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White appears; it is not an anticoagulant. The preferred anticoagulants in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation are direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban. Tell: procainamide treats the rhythm; apixaban prevents clots.

Correct. Apixaban is one of the direct oral anticoagulants preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, along with dabigatran, edoxaban and rivaroxaban. Patients typically require anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high, and stroke risk is assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score.

Warfarin can be used for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation, with a target international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3, but it is not a direct oral anticoagulant. The preferred direct oral anticoagulants are dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban and rivaroxaban. Tell: warfarin needs a ratio target; the preferred drugs are the direct agents.

Aspirin is not among the anticoagulants listed for atrial fibrillation, and it appears on the HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score as a medication that predisposes to bleeding. The preferred agents are direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban. Tell: aspirin raises bleeding risk; apixaban is the preferred anticoagulant.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. This patient has a fast atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, the opposite problem, which is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: atropine is for a slow rate; procainamide is for pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. When adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals this combination, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated. Tell: pre-excited atrial fibrillation has one named drug answer, procainamide.

Correct. Slowing from adenosine has unmasked atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, and in that setting intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine. The same rule applies whenever Wolff-Parkinson-White is already known; adenosine stays first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry.

A repeat dose of adenosine is allowed for ordinary stable supraventricular tachycardia, but once atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is revealed, adenosine must never be used. Intravenous procainamide takes its place. Tell: the moment a pre-excited atrial fibrillation appears, adenosine is off the table.

set1.q: What defines inappropriate sinus tachycardia?
opts: A fast rate from fever or infection is a response to an underlying pathologic condition, which makes it appropriate sinus tachycardia, managed by treating the cause. Inappropriate means no cause remains after all are excluded. Tell: an identifiable cause makes the tachycardia appropriate.

Tachycardia during exercise is a normal physiologic response, an appropriate sinus tachycardia. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia persists with no cause found after secondary causes are excluded. Tell: exercise explains the rate, so it is appropriate.

A sinus tachycardia from stimulants or other medication effects is explained and therefore appropriate. Inappropriate means the elevated rate stays unexplained once such causes are excluded. Tell: any identified drug or illness cause rules out the inappropriate label.

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is an elevated heart rate that remains unexplained after secondary causes have been excluded, so it is a diagnosis of exclusion. It is generally left untreated, because patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment and the prognosis is usually benign.

set1.q: What is the tachy-brady form of sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Slowing on expiration, speeding up on inspiration

A rate that rises with inspiration and falls with expiration is sinus arrhythmia, a normal, physiologic rhythm with uniform P waves. Tachy-brady syndrome alternates a tachyarrhythmia with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses. Tell: breathing-linked variation is normal; fast-slow swings with pauses are sick sinus syndrome.
Fast atrial rhythms alternating with slow ones

Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome, fast atrial rhythms alternate with slow rhythms or pauses: a tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses. It is one of the three forms of sick sinus syndrome, with sinus exit block and sinus arrest.
An impulse that cannot exit the node

An impulse that is generated but cannot get out of the sinus node is sinus node exit block, another form of sick sinus syndrome. Tachy-brady syndrome instead alternates fast atrial rhythms with slow rhythms or pauses. Tell: exit block is a trapped impulse; tachy-brady is a fast-slow alternation.
An impulse the node fails to generate

An impulse the sinus node never generates is sinus arrest, the form of sick sinus syndrome that leads to a junctional rhythm. Tachy-brady syndrome alternates fast atrial rhythms with slow rhythms or pauses. Tell: arrest means no impulse; tachy-brady means swings between fast and slow.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which medication class is a recognized cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Stimulants are a listed drug cause of sinus tachycardia, not bradycardia. The drug causes of sinus bradycardia are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. Tell: stimulants speed the sinus node.

Beta-agonists are listed triggers of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a fast rhythm. It is beta blockers, the opposite class, that slow the sinus rate. Tell: an agonist speeds things up; a blocker slows them down.

Correct. Beta blockers are a listed medication cause of sinus bradycardia, along with nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. The non-drug causes include hypothyroidism, sinus node ischemia, increased intracranial pressure and late-stage infection.

Anticholinergic drugs are a listed cause of sinus tachycardia, as stimulants are. The medication causes of sinus bradycardia are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin. Tell: anticholinergics sit on the fast list.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: What is the usual rate of a junctional rhythm?
opts: Correct. A junctional rhythm is regular, usually at 40 to 60, with a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds and P waves that are inverted in II, III and aVF before the QRS, buried in it or after it, with a short or absent PR.

A rate of 60 to 100 is the normal sinus range, and also the underlying rate listed for premature junctional contractions, which are early beats on a normal rhythm. A sustained junctional rhythm is slower, usually 40 to 60. Tell: a junctional rhythm is a slow rhythm.

Over 100 up to 160 is the range of sinus tachycardia, a regular sinus rhythm with a P wave before every QRS. A junctional rhythm is slow, usually 40 to 60, with inverted or hidden P waves. Tell: a junctional rhythm sits below 60, not above 100.

An atrial rate of 250 or more, approaching 300, describes atrial flutter, with sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes. A junctional rhythm usually runs at 40 to 60. Tell: 250 to 300 is flutter; 40 to 60 is junctional.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which counseling fits benign premature atrial contractions?
opts: Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Benign premature atrial contractions are managed with trigger avoidance and reassurance. Tell: isolated early beats bring no anticoagulation decision.

A beta blocker such as metoprolol is used only when premature atrial contractions are persistent and symptomatic. Benign beats are managed with reassurance and trigger avoidance. Tell: counseling comes first; drugs are for persistent symptoms.

Correct. For premature atrial contractions in a normal heart, counsel the patient to avoid potential precipitants such as excessive alcohol, stress and caffeine, and give reassurance about the benign nature of the rhythm. Most people are asymptomatic, and no treatment is needed if there are no symptoms.

Stopping exercise is not part of the counseling for premature atrial contractions. The advice is to avoid precipitants such as excessive alcohol, stress and caffeine, with reassurance about the benign rhythm. Tell: the listed triggers are alcohol, stress and caffeine, not exercise.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which therapy is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome. Focal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm from a single ectopic focus, and catheter ablation is usually curative. Tell: pacemakers support slow rhythms; ablation removes a fast focus.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. Focal atrial tachycardia is fast, and it is cured by catheter ablation in about 90 percent. Tell: atropine raises a slow rate; it cannot cure a tachycardia.

Correct. Catheter ablation is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia, in about 90 percent. For chronic management an oral beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is the initial therapy, but ablation is the step that cures the ectopic focus.

Adenosine is a diagnostic tool in focal atrial tachycardia because it is usually less effective at terminating it than node-dependent reentry. A drug that usually fails to stop the rhythm cannot cure it; catheter ablation can. Tell: adenosine helps diagnose; ablation cures.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which rhythm describes atrial fibrillation?
opts: Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and an absent PR interval, with a narrow QRS. Its rate is usually 110 to 160 but not always, and can fall below 80 or rise above 200, so the rhythm and the missing P waves identify it, not the rate.

A regular rhythm with sawtooth waves describes atrial flutter, at an atrial rate of 250 or more with more flutter waves than QRS complexes. Atrial fibrillation has no organized atrial waves and is irregularly irregular. Tell: sawtooth and regular is flutter.

An irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes describes multifocal atrial tachycardia, which still has a P wave before every QRS. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves at all. Tell: in an irregular rhythm, P waves in several shapes mean multifocal; absent P waves mean fibrillation.

A regular narrow rhythm with hidden P waves describes a reentrant supraventricular tachycardia such as nodal reentry. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular. Tell: both may lack visible P waves, so regularity decides it.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which type of atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is more common?
opts: Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia comes in orthodromic and antidromic forms, and orthodromic is more common. Orthodromic reentry uses antegrade conduction through the atrioventricular node, giving a regular, narrow complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave after the QRS.

Antidromic reentry is the less common form, and it gives a wide QRS complex instead of the narrow complex of orthodromic reentry. Its circuit runs the other way, with retrograde conduction through the atrioventricular node. Tell: orthodromic is common and narrow; antidromic is uncommon and wide.

Multifocal describes an atrial tachycardia with at least three P-wave shapes from multiple foci, not a type of accessory pathway reentry. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia comes as orthodromic or antidromic. Tell: multifocal is a focus label; orthodromic and antidromic are reentry directions.

Slow-fast is the most common, typical type of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a circuit within the node. Accessory pathway reentry is classed instead as orthodromic or antidromic. Tell: slow-fast names nodal reentry; orthodromic names the common accessory pathway form.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: What is the cure rate of catheter ablation for atrioventricular nodal reentry?
opts: About 50 percent badly undersells it. Catheter ablation offers a select subset of patients with nodal reentry a definitive cure in over 95 percent. Tell: over 95 percent is the nodal reentry ablation figure, a near-certain cure rather than a coin flip.

About 70 percent is too low. Ablation for nodal reentry offers selected patients a definitive cure in over 95 percent. Tell: remember nodal reentry ablation as near-certain, over 95 percent, a step above the roughly 90 percent quoted for focal atrial tachycardia.

About 90 percent is the cure rate quoted for catheter ablation of focal atrial tachycardia. Ablation for atrioventricular nodal reentry does better, over 95 percent. Tell: focal atrial tachycardia 90 percent, nodal reentry over 95 percent.

Correct. Catheter ablation offers a select subset of patients with atrioventricular nodal reentry the opportunity for a definitive cure, in over 95 percent. Most episodes are otherwise well tolerated and almost always end with vagal maneuvers or adenosine.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: How does the rhythm of multifocal atrial tachycardia compare with focal atrial tachycardia?
opts: This reverses them. The single focus of focal atrial tachycardia gives a regular rhythm, and the multiple foci of multifocal atrial tachycardia give an irregular one. Tell: more foci means more variability, so multifocal is the irregular one.

Only focal atrial tachycardia is regular. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in the same lead from multiple foci. Tell: changing P shapes go with changing intervals.

Both rhythms have one P wave for every QRS; focal shows one consistent abnormal shape and multifocal at least three changing shapes. Absent P waves describe atrial fibrillation. Tell: in an irregular narrow rhythm, absent P waves mean fibrillation and several P shapes mean multifocal.

Correct. Focal atrial tachycardia is regular because a single ectopic focus drives it, while multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three distinct P-wave shapes in the same lead from multiple foci. Both keep one P wave for every QRS, with a constant PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.

Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set2.q: How do most people with premature junctional contractions present?
opts: Syncope is not the usual picture of premature junctional contractions, which most people do not notice at all. Management is reassurance when they are infrequent and asymptomatic, with a beta blocker only for persistent symptoms. Tell: these early beats are mostly silent and benign.

Chest pain is not the typical presentation; most people with premature junctional contractions are not symptomatic. Frequent beats, over 10 per minute or multifocal, prompt a search for structural heart disease. Tell: the usual presentation is no symptoms at all, often found on a monitor.

Stroke risk drives anticoagulation decisions in atrial fibrillation, assessed with a stroke-risk score; it is not how premature junctional contractions present. Most people with these beats are not symptomatic. Tell: occasional junctional early beats are benign and usually silent.

Correct. Most people with premature junctional contractions are not symptomatic. No treatment is needed if the beats are asymptomatic and infrequent, and reassurance of the benign nature of the rhythm is often enough; a beta blocker is kept for persistent symptoms or frequent beats.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: How common is hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Instability is not the usual picture: unstable supraventricular tachycardia is the less common presentation. Patients may be asymptomatic or have transient palpitations, lightheadedness or chest discomfort. Tell: most supraventricular tachycardia is stable, which is why the first-line steps are a vagal maneuver and adenosine.
Tied to a wide QRS complex

Supraventricular tachycardias are by definition narrow QRS complex rhythms, with antidromic atrioventricular reentry the wide exception, and instability is not tied to QRS width. Collapse usually needs a heart rate above 200. Tell: think rate, not width, when predicting instability in supraventricular tachycardia.

Symptoms may be more pronounced in elderly patients or those with structural heart disease, but instability is not mainly an older-adult event. It is the less common presentation overall and usually needs a rate above 200. Tell: age worsens symptoms; a rate above 200 drives collapse.

Correct. Hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia is the less common presentation. Many patients are asymptomatic or have transient symptoms if it is paroxysmal, and supraventricular tachycardia usually does not lead to syncope or hemodynamic collapse unless the heart rate goes above 200.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which is a physiologic cause of sinus tachycardia?
opts: Correct. Sinus tachycardia is classed by cause, and pain and anxiety are the listed physiologic causes, along with exercise and conditions that raise catecholamine release. Physiologic sinus tachycardia usually comes without symptoms such as dizziness or nausea, and it settles when the cause is treated.

Hypovolemia is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, together with hypotension or shock, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction and hyperthyroidism. The question asks for a physiologic cause. Tell: physiologic means a normal response such as pain, anxiety or exercise; disease states are pathologic.

Pulmonary embolism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, like myocardial infarction and hypoxia. The physiologic causes are normal responses such as pain and anxiety. Tell: if the cause is a disease process, the sinus tachycardia is pathologic.

Hyperthyroidism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, a disease state rather than a normal response. Physiologic sinus tachycardia comes from pain, anxiety or exercise. Tell: endocrine disease belongs on the pathologic list, not the physiologic one.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Sinus tachycardia is defined by a sinus rate in which range?
opts: A rate of 60 to 100 is the normal sinus range, also the range of sinus arrhythmia. Sinus tachycardia begins above 100 and runs up to 160. Tell: under 60 is sinus bradycardia, 60 to 100 is normal, and over 100 up to 160 is sinus tachycardia.

Correct. Sinus tachycardia is a regular sinus rhythm above 100 up to 160, with a uniform P wave for every QRS, a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds and a narrow QRS. Above 160, a regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves is described as supraventricular tachycardia.

Above 160, a regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves is described as supraventricular tachycardia, not sinus tachycardia. Sinus tachycardia keeps a P wave for every QRS and runs above 100 up to 160. Tell: the sinus tachycardia ceiling is 160.

An atrial rate of 250 or more, approaching 300, describes atrial flutter, with sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes. Sinus tachycardia runs above 100 up to 160 with one P wave per QRS. Tell: 250 to 300 is a flutter number, not a sinus one.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: When is catheter ablation used for premature atrial contractions?
opts: Most people with premature atrial contractions are asymptomatic, and asymptomatic beats get no treatment at all. Ablation is kept for frequent beats or beats that trigger atrial fibrillation. Tell: finding premature atrial beats is not by itself a reason for any procedure.

Asymptomatic premature atrial contractions get no treatment, which is the opposite of an ablation indication. Ablation is for frequent beats or those triggering atrial fibrillation. Tell: no symptoms means no treatment.

Premature atrial contractions brought on by caffeine, alcohol or stress in a normal heart are managed by counseling to avoid the trigger and reassurance about the benign rhythm. Ablation is for frequent beats or those triggering atrial fibrillation. Tell: a removable trigger calls for avoidance, not ablation.

Correct. Catheter ablation is used when premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation. Otherwise, persistent symptomatic beats get a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated, and asymptomatic ones get no treatment.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: In hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation, what is the first aim of management?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. Stable atrial fibrillation is an irregular rhythm whose first aim is rate control. Tell: pacemakers are for slow rhythms, not the opening move in atrial fibrillation.

Correct. In hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation the first aim is rate control, given intravenously if the patient is in rapid ventricular response, with anticoagulation planned for all. Rhythm options such as outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation, or mapping and ablation, come later.

Immediate conversion, by synchronized cardioversion, is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation. In a stable patient, elective conversion comes later as an outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: stable means rate control first; immediate conversion needs instability.

Mapping and ablation is a later option in atrial fibrillation, not the first aim. A stable patient is managed first with rate control, intravenous if in rapid ventricular response. Tell: procedures come after the rate is controlled.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which trigger can precipitate atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia?
opts: Increased vagal tone causes slow rhythms, such as junctional rhythm in well-conditioned athletes, and vagal maneuvers almost always terminate nodal reentry. It ends this tachycardia rather than starting it. Tell: vagal stimulation is the treatment; caffeine and sympathomimetics are the triggers.

Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is commonly seen without heart disease and may occur spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics. Caffeine is therefore a listed trigger, and patients typically report sudden palpitations with neck pulsations (frog sign).

Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, conditions that slow the heart. It is not among the triggers of nodal reentry. Tell: the triggers of nodal reentry are things that speed the heart, like caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists and sympathomimetics.

Beta blockers are used against nodal reentry, as a pill-in-the-pocket option along with nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. It is beta-agonists, the opposite class, that can trigger it. Tell: a beta-agonist triggers it; a beta blocker treats it.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
set2.q: Besides athletes and sleepers, which adult group commonly shows sinus bradycardia?
opts: Correct. Sinus bradycardia can be a normal variant, seen as an adaptive response in well-conditioned or active people, during sleep, and in adults over age 65. Most people with it are asymptomatic, and asymptomatic sinus bradycardia is not treated.

Anxiety is a listed physiologic cause of sinus tachycardia, which raises the sinus rate. The adult group listed for sinus bradycardia is those over 65. Tell: anxiety speeds the heart; older age is on the slow list.

Hyperthyroidism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, speeding the sinus rate; it is hypothyroidism that appears among the causes of sinus bradycardia. The listed adult group is those over 65. Tell: thyroid excess is fast, thyroid deficiency is slow.

Stimulants are a listed drug cause of sinus tachycardia, raising the sinus rate. The adult group in which sinus bradycardia is commonly seen is those over 65. Tell: stimulants belong on the fast list, with anticholinergics.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which electrocardiogram pattern defines sinus arrhythmia?
opts: Irregularly irregular with no P waves

An irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves describes atrial fibrillation. Sinus arrhythmia keeps a uniform P wave before every QRS, and its irregularity follows breathing. Tell: patterned irregularity with P waves is sinus arrhythmia; patternless irregularity without them is fibrillation.

A regular rhythm with sawtooth baseline waves describes atrial flutter, at an atrial rate of 250 or more. Sinus arrhythmia is irregular, following breathing, with normal sinus P waves. Tell: a sawtooth baseline means flutter, never sinus arrhythmia.

At least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead with an irregular rhythm describes multifocal atrial tachycardia, a rate over 100 from multiple foci. Sinus arrhythmia keeps one uniform P-wave shape at 60 to 100. Tell: the P-wave shape stays constant in sinus arrhythmia; only the timing varies.

Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern, faster with inspiration and slower with expiration, at 60 to 100. A uniform P wave precedes every narrow QRS with a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, so only the spacing of the beats changes.

set2.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, a fast rhythm, and is not used to raise a slow rate. Unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker. Tell: amiodarone belongs to the fast-rhythm toolbox; atropine to the slow.

A permanent pacemaker is the treatment for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first step in an acute, unstable episode. The acute sequence is atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine; chronic and symptomatic means a permanent pacemaker.

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine. If it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows; chronic symptomatic bradycardia is managed with a permanent pacemaker, and asymptomatic bradycardia is not treated at all.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Slowing a heart that is already too slow and causing instability is the opposite of the goal. Tell: adenosine treats fast narrow rhythms; atropine treats unstable slow ones.

set2.q: Which drug is used for persistent symptoms from premature junctional contractions?
opts: Correct. If symptoms from premature junctional contractions persist, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is used if not contraindicated; frequent beats, over 10 per minute or multifocal, are also treated with a beta blocker after a search for heart disease. Infrequent, asymptomatic beats need only reassurance.

Adenosine is used in stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. It is not the listed treatment for premature junctional contractions. Tell: persistent symptoms from junctional early beats are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, and it is also used for junctional rhythm from digitalis toxicity. Persistent symptoms from premature junctional contractions are instead treated with metoprolol. Tell: atropine raises a slow rate; a beta blocker settles symptomatic early beats.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Premature junctional contractions with persistent symptoms are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol. Tell: procainamide belongs to pre-excited atrial fibrillation, not to junctional beats.

set2.q: After how much anticoagulation can stable atrial fibrillation be electively cardioverted as an outpatient?
opts: A single day of anticoagulation is far short of the listed interval. Elective outpatient cardioversion of stable atrial fibrillation follows 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: remember three weeks, 21 days, before an elective outpatient cardioversion.

Correct. Elective outpatient cardioversion of atrial fibrillation follows 21 days of anticoagulation, the same interval used before elective cardioversion of atrial flutter. Anticoagulation is part of management for all patients with atrial fibrillation, guided by the stroke-risk and bleeding-risk scores.

Three months is longer than the listed interval. Elective outpatient cardioversion of stable atrial fibrillation can follow 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: the number to remember is 21 days, about three weeks, not three months.

A year of anticoagulation is not required first; one year is instead the cutoff that separates persistent from long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation. Elective outpatient cardioversion follows 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: 21 days before cardioversion; one year is a duration category.

set2.q: Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia depends on which structure?
opts: Three or more atrial foci, shown as at least three P-wave shapes in one lead, make multifocal atrial tachycardia, an irregular rhythm in acutely ill patients. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia instead depends on an accessory pathway. Tell: multiple foci means multifocal; an extra pathway means atrioventricular reentry.

A damaged sinus node, from ischemia or cardiac surgery, produces sick sinus syndrome with pauses, arrest or tachy-brady swings. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia depends on an accessory pathway, not on sinus node failure. Tell: a failing sinus node gives slow rhythms and pauses; a pathway gives reentry.

Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is seen in patients with an accessory pathway, such as in Wolff-Parkinson-White, and the reentry circuit uses that pathway alongside the atrioventricular node. Pre-excitation on a sinus tracing, a short PR and delta wave, signals the pathway, and ablating it is first-line long-term treatment.

A reentry circuit confined within the atrioventricular node is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, which needs no accessory pathway. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia, without the word nodal, uses an accessory pathway. Tell: nodal reentry stays inside the node; atrioventricular reentry needs the bundle of Kent.

set2.q: What is the definitive management of atrial flutter?
opts: Vagal maneuvers are first line for stable supraventricular tachycardia and almost always terminate nodal reentry, but they are not the listed management of atrial flutter. Flutter is rate controlled when stable and treated definitively by ablation. Tell: definitive means the step that ends recurrences, which is ablation.

Correct. Ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter. Flutter has a substantial recurrence rate and is harder to rate control than atrial fibrillation, so although stable patients start with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker, ablation is what ends the problem.

Adenosine follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia and may slow the rate enough to reveal atrial activity, but it is not a cure for flutter. Ablation is the definitive management. Tell: adenosine acts acutely; ablation is definitive.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome. Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm, managed with rate control or cardioversion and treated definitively by ablation. Tell: a pacemaker supports slow rates; it does not end flutter.

set2.q: Which cardiac event is a listed cause of junctional rhythm?
opts: Hypovolemia and hypotension or shock are listed pathologic causes of sinus tachycardia, which speeds the sinus node. They are not causes of junctional rhythm. Tell: junctional rhythm follows a slowed or failed sinus node, inferior infarction, cardiac surgery or digoxin toxicity.

Hyperthyroidism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, raising the sinus rate. A junctional rhythm takes over when the sinus node fails or slows, as with sick sinus syndrome or significant bradycardia. Tell: a fast sinus node does not hand over to the junction.

Correct. Inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, alongside sinus node dysfunction such as sick sinus syndrome, significant bradycardia, the acute period after cardiac surgery and digoxin toxicity. Junctional rhythm can also appear in healthy athletes with high vagal tone and is generally well tolerated.

Pulmonary embolism is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, not of junctional rhythm. The listed cardiac event behind junctional rhythm is inferior myocardial infarction. Tell: pulmonary embolism speeds the sinus node; inferior infarction can let the junction take over.

set2.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Sinus tachycardia is regular, at over 100 to 160, with a uniform P wave before every QRS. This fast run is irregularly irregular with no P waves, so it is not coming from the sinus node. Tell: a P wave before every beat keeps the rhythm sinus; irregularity without P waves means atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome, and then the patient needs a permanent pacemaker with an implantable defibrillator. But ventricular tachycardia is regular, at about 150 to 200, while this run is irregularly irregular with no P waves. Tell: an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which a tachyarrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses, atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of the fast rhythm.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is also irregular, but each QRS has a P wave, in at least three different shapes in the same lead. A fast run with no P waves at all is atrial fibrillation, the most common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. Tell: P waves present in several shapes means multifocal; absent P waves means fibrillation.

set2.q: When premature junctional contractions are frequent (over 10 per minute), what is done?
opts: Correct. Premature junctional contractions that are frequent, over 10 per minute or multifocal, prompt a look for underlying structural heart disease, and the beats are treated with a beta blocker. By contrast, infrequent beats without symptoms need no treatment beyond reassurance.

Reassurance alone suits premature junctional contractions that are infrequent and asymptomatic. At over 10 per minute they are frequent, which prompts a search for structural heart disease. Tell: the threshold is more than 10 per minute or multifocal.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Frequent premature junctional contractions lead instead to a search for structural heart disease and a beta blocker. Tell: early junctional beats carry no anticoagulation decision.

A permanent pacemaker is for slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm caused by complete or high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome. Frequent premature junctional contractions are early beats, handled with a structural workup and a beta blocker. Tell: premature beats are not bradycardia, so no device.

set2.q: In sinus arrest, which rhythm may take over?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is not the rhythm listed as taking over in sinus arrest. When the sinus node stops generating impulses, a junctional rhythm takes over, narrow and usually 40 to 60. Tell: sinus arrest leads to slow, narrow junctional beats with inverted or hidden P waves.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia comes from three or more atrial foci in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. It is not the rhythm that follows sinus arrest, which is junctional. Tell: after a pause with no sinus impulse, expect slow narrow junctional beats, not a fast atrial rhythm.

Correct. In sinus arrest the sinus node does not generate an impulse, which leads to a junctional rhythm taking over, typically at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves. This differs from sinus exit block, in which the impulse is generated but cannot get out of the node.

Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm with sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more. Sinus arrest, in which the sinus node generates no impulse, leads instead to a junctional rhythm. Tell: sinus arrest is followed by slow narrow beats, not by sawtooth waves.

set2.q: Atrial flutter is commonly seen in which patients?
opts: Increased intracranial pressure is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, a slow sinus rhythm. Atrial flutter is linked to atrial scarring, right-sided heart failure and pulmonary vascular disease. Tell: raised intracranial pressure slows the sinus node; it does not create flutter.

Correct. Atrial flutter is commonly seen in patients with atrial scarring or damage, for example after surgery, as well as with right-sided heart failure or pulmonary vascular disease, and in patients with atrial fibrillation who are taking an antiarrhythmic.

Caffeine in young women without heart disease is the classic setting of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. Atrial flutter is instead commonly seen with atrial scarring or damage, right-sided heart failure or pulmonary vascular disease. Tell: flutter goes with damaged atria and right-sided disease.

Healthy, well-conditioned athletes commonly show sinus bradycardia or junctional rhythm from increased vagal tone. Atrial flutter is commonly seen with atrial scarring after surgery, right-sided heart failure or pulmonary vascular disease. Tell: athletes slow down; scarred atria flutter.

set2.q: Which is a recognized cause of sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Caffeine is a listed trigger of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia and of premature atrial contractions in normal hearts. It is not among the causes of sick sinus syndrome. Tell: caffeine provokes fast rhythms; sick sinus syndrome comes from node damage, drugs, electrolytes or hypothyroidism.

Correct. Listed causes of sick sinus syndrome include sinoatrial node ischemia, injury to the sinoatrial node from cardiac surgery, electrolyte abnormalities, medications such as beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin, and hypothyroidism. Management starts with treating the underlying cause.

It is hypothyroidism, not excess thyroid hormone, that is listed as a cause of sick sinus syndrome; hyperthyroidism is instead a listed cause of sinus tachycardia. Tell: an underactive thyroid slows the sinus node; an overactive one speeds it.

Anemia is a listed pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, a compensatory fast rhythm. The listed causes of sick sinus syndrome are node ischemia or surgical injury, electrolyte abnormalities, medications and hypothyroidism. Tell: anemia speeds the sinus node rather than damaging it.

set2.q: What is the management of asymptomatic sinus bradycardia?
opts: Correct. Sinus bradycardia can be a normal variant, and most people with it are asymptomatic; no treatment is given if there are no symptoms. Atropine, then a temporary pacemaker, is for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, and a permanent pacemaker for chronic symptomatic disease.

Atropine is first line only for acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. An asymptomatic patient is left untreated. Tell: no symptoms, no atropine; the treatment ladder starts only when symptoms and instability appear.

A temporary pacemaker follows atropine in an acute, symptomatic, unstable patient. It has no place when the bradycardia causes no symptoms. Tell: the whole treatment ladder starts only once symptoms appear.

A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia. Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia, common in athletes, during sleep and in adults over 65, is not treated. Tell: a permanent pacemaker needs chronic symptoms.

set2.q: What does a premature junctional contraction look like?
opts: Early narrow QRS, P inverted or hidden

Correct. A premature junctional contraction begins within the atrioventricular junction and gives an early, narrow QRS, usually 0.10 seconds or less, with an inverted P wave, a P wave buried in the QRS (appearing as no P wave) or a P wave after the QRS.
Early wide QRS without a P wave

An early, wide and bizarre QRS with no P wave describes a premature ventricular contraction, which begins within the ventricles. A junctional early beat keeps a narrow QRS. Tell: wide and bizarre is ventricular; narrow with an inverted or hidden P wave is junctional.

An early, abnormally shaped P wave before a narrow QRS describes a premature atrial contraction, which begins in the atria. A junctional early beat has an inverted P wave, a hidden one or one after the QRS. Tell: an abnormal P wave in front means atrial; inverted, hidden or trailing means junctional.

Sawtooth waves before the QRS belong to atrial flutter, with an atrial rate of 250 or more. A premature junctional contraction is a single early narrow beat with an inverted, buried or trailing P wave. Tell: sawtooth means flutter; one early narrow beat means an ectopic.

set2.q: Which type of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is most common?
opts: Orthodromic and antidromic are the two forms of atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia through an accessory pathway, and orthodromic is the more common of those. They are not types of nodal reentry. Tell: orthodromic and antidromic describe accessory pathway reentry; slow-fast describes nodal reentry.

Antidromic is the less common form of accessory pathway reentry and the wide-complex exception among supraventricular tachycardias. It is not a type of nodal reentry. Tell: antidromic means a wide accessory pathway rhythm; the most common nodal type is slow-fast.

Correct. Slow-fast, or typical, atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is the most common type of nodal reentry. It is a regular, narrow complex tachycardia, usually 140 to 180, with hidden P waves from a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node.

The most common type of atrioventricular nodal reentry is named slow-fast, also called typical; fast-slow is not the listed common type. Both names describe nodal reentry, so the order of the words is the whole question. Tell: typical nodal reentry is slow, then fast.

set2.q: How do patients with atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia most commonly present?
opts: Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is seen in patients with an accessory pathway, such as Wolff-Parkinson-White, and patients most commonly present with palpitations. The rhythm is regular, usually 200 to 300, with hidden or retrograde P waves.

Stroke risk is what anticoagulation addresses in atrial fibrillation, assessed with a stroke-risk score; it is not how reentrant tachycardia presents. Patients with atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia most commonly present with palpitations. Tell: a fast regular reentry rhythm is felt as palpitations.

Heart failure is not the usual presentation; patients with atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia most commonly present with palpitations. Heart failure appears instead among the causes of multifocal atrial tachycardia. Tell: the classic complaint in accessory pathway reentry is palpitations.

Reentry through an accessory pathway produces a tachycardia, above 100 and usually 200 to 300, felt as palpitations. Bradycardia belongs to sinus node disease or drug effects. Tell: reentry means fast, so the presentation is palpitations.

set2.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: Correct. In stable supraventricular tachycardia, the narrow complex tachycardias, a vagal maneuver is first line, before any drug. Adenosine follows if needed, may be repeated once, and may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.

An echocardiogram is not part of the acute sequence for stable supraventricular tachycardia, which runs vagal maneuver, then adenosine. The question asks for the step before any drug, and that is the vagal maneuver. Tell: the first move in a stable narrow tachycardia is a bedside, drug-free maneuver.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is not a first step. Stable narrow complex tachycardia begins with a vagal maneuver. Tell: procainamide answers pre-excited atrial fibrillation; a stable narrow tachycardia starts drug-free.

Synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage, is immediate treatment only for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. A stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine. Tell: the word stable in the question takes the shock off the table.

set2.q: What is a delta wave?
opts: An inverted T wave is a change after the QRS, at the end of the complex. The delta wave sits at the very start of the QRS, as a slurred upstroke. Tell: look at the beginning of the QRS for a delta wave, not at the T wave.

A sawtooth baseline is the flutter wave of atrial flutter, at an atrial rate of 250 or more. The delta wave is a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS. Tell: sawtooth means flutter; a slurred QRS onset means pre-excitation.
A slurred upstroke of the QRS

Correct. A delta wave is a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS complex. With a short PR interval under 0.12 seconds and a wide QRS, it marks pre-excitation from an accessory pathway in Wolff-Parkinson-White.

A notched or widened P wave is a change in the P wave, before the QRS. The delta wave is part of the QRS itself, a slurred upstroke at its start, paired with a short PR interval. Tell: the delta wave belongs to the QRS, not to the P wave.

set2.q: Which pair are both listed risk factors for atrial fibrillation?
opts: Older age, not youth, is the listed age-related risk for atrial fibrillation, and female sex is not on that list, though it adds a point to the stroke-risk score. Tell: atrial fibrillation risks are hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, family history, obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol and older age.

Obesity, not low weight, is the listed weight-related risk for atrial fibrillation, and anemia is a listed cause of sinus tachycardia instead. Tell: the atrial fibrillation list includes obesity and sleep apnea, along with hypertension and diabetes.

Correct. Hypertension and diabetes are both listed; atrial fibrillation is commonly seen in patients with hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, a family history of atrial fibrillation, obesity, sleep apnea, excessive alcohol and older age.

Neither is on the atrial fibrillation list. Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, and it is high blood pressure, not low, that is a listed risk. Tell: the pair on the list is hypertension and diabetes.

set2.q: An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 appears in someone with a known accessory pathway. Which intravenous drug is used?
opts: Adenosine must never be used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White appears; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. This irregular, wide rhythm with a known accessory pathway is that exception. Tell: a known accessory pathway plus a fast irregular rhythm rules adenosine out.

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, a slow rhythm. This tachycardia already approaches 300, the opposite problem. Tell: atropine is for slow and unstable rhythms; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.

Intravenous magnesium is not the listed drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. An irregular, wide tachycardia in someone with a known accessory pathway is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: a known pathway plus irregular wide complexes means procainamide.

Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 in someone with a known accessory pathway is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. When Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, intravenous procainamide is used, and adenosine must never be given.
